findings.where: Screen 6 words and the Volts to drive 5 A readout
findings.what: "Shorted, it needs just 1.0 V" comes from the CT's own 0.2 Ω winding, which no screen mentions until screen 7's question, so Dan expects 0 V for a shorted meter circuit; add "Its own winding has 0.2 Ω, so even shorted it needs 5 × 0.2 = 1.0 V" and trim elsewhere to stay under 90 words.
"So this is why an open CT is dangerous" comes straight after the auto-transformer's 26% and 74% split, so the "So" follows from nothing; drop the repeated CT recap or move it into the CT paragraph.

"Its ampere-turns cancel the busbar's" is followed by "So the core needs only enough flux", but exact cancelling would leave nothing to make that flux; say "almost cancel", as the explain does, and that the small difference makes the flux.

"The supply's current flows straight on into the load. That carries 115 ÷ 440 of the power" skips the step that the supply current is the power ÷ 440 and arrives at 115 V, so it carries 115 ÷ 440 of the power; one short sentence completes the why that screen 11 relies on.

No screen says why the split matters: only the transformed share needs a transformer's iron and copper, so an auto is much smaller only near a 1:1 ratio and saves just about a quarter at 440 V to 115 V; without it the isolating-against-auto trade shows only the auto's cost, and the 9% puzzle has no point.

"It rises while the voltage is positive, so it peaks at each voltage zero" and "The next half-cycle still adds two peaks' worth" skip the step that at a rising zero the flux normally sits at its lowest peak and each half-cycle swings it from one peak to the other; one sentence makes the doubling something he can say back.

The brief promised a mixed set from the whole course, but all three are from this lesson. Screen 12 also reuses screen 6's own CT (400 A, one turn, 5 A), so he can recall 80 instead of working it out. Use a different CT ratio, and swap one puzzle for a lesson 4 to 7 idea such as turns ratio, efficiency, regulation or vector group.

findings.where: Whole lesson against the brief's row 8
findings.what: The brief's uses are missing from screens, explain and practice: isolated distribution fed by transformers, two independent transformers, the ship side of shore power, and an ungrounded system needing a fully insulated winding (the last ties straight to his insulated systems course); so is the named-only transformer protection and PI test.

The VT is first met in the final quiz, and only its stem teaches it; a sentence on screen 8 or in screen 9's why (a VT is fed a voltage, so open is safe and a short is a fault) would let the last puzzle test something taught.

Two sliders and a Switch on button appear but no sentence invites him to use them; add one such as "Try other moments and flux left in, then switch on again", with a read sentence that works with no controls.

findings.where: Switch-on card readouts and screen 2 read
findings.what: "12.02 × full load" and "9.91 × full load" give two decimals from a sketch whose past-the-knee slope of 15 was chosen for the picture; whole numbers past the knee (12, 21, 24) would be honest, keeping 0.02 below it.

findings.where: Switch-on card, B-H sketch (360 light and dark moved)
findings.what: The Flux axis is drawn at −3 times full load, not at zero current, so the curve's steep part runs as a separate vertical line beside the axis instead of up it; put the axis at zero current.
"That is 13% of the knee" cannot be checked by hand because no screen gives the 30 V knee; say "of the 30 V knee".
"The first close caught a worse moment on the wave" leaves out the flux left in, though the picture shows 0.8 left in; say "a worse moment on the wave, with flux left in the same way".

"A breaker that trips once on switch-on and holds on the next try usually points to inrush. If it trips again, treat it as a fault" has no source for "usually" and reads as permission for one free re-close. Keep to what the source says: inrush can trip protection and look like an internal fault. Then say to find which protection operated before closing again.
Six footnote marks, four on explanations rather than values he would look up ([^1] saturation as the cause, [^3], [^4], [^6]); keep [^2] for 8 to 30 times and [^5] for 4000 V.
"Still there." reads oddly on its own; a line such as "Right, you still have it." says what it means.
